summary.en: The United States has revived a torture indictment against Maduro for ordering torture of rivals and deployed Space Force electromagnetic and electronic warfare systems against Venezuela while pressuring Reliance to refine Venezuelan oil. Opposition groups are staging nationwide protests demanding elections and the return of Machado, and a Dutch security report warns that Venezuela’s instability could threaten Curaçao and the wider Caribbean Kingdom. The Pentagon has issued a directive banning DoD personnel from using nonpublic information to bet on U.S. military operations involving Venezuela, and the U.S. Embassy has reopened in Venezuela to full staff. There were 2 battle-related deaths in 2007, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: USA har gjenopptatt en torturanklage mot Maduro for å ha beordret tortur av rivaler og har satt i drift elektromagnetiske og elektroniske krigssystemer fra Space Force mot Venezuela mens de presser Reliance til å raffinere venezuelansk olje. Opposisjonsgrupper holder landsomfattende protester som krever valg og at Machado kommer tilbake, og en nederlandsk sikkerhetsrapport advarer om at Venezuelas ustabilitet kan true Curaçao og det bredere Karibiske kongeriket. Pentagon har gitt en instruks om at DoD-personell ikke får bruke ikke-offentlig informasjon til å satse på amerikanske militæroperasjoner som involverer Venezuela, og den amerikanske ambassaden har gjenåpnet i Venezuela med fullt personale. Det var 2 dødsfall i kamp i 2007, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro and Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
